summary: An experimental document that defines how Internet Printing Protocol operations and attributes are encoded in a new media type, application/ipp, and how a message with this type is transported over HTTP. It was replaced by RFC 2910.

eli5.summary: This says how to pack print requests into a standard envelope and send them over the web to a printer.

questions: how does internet printing protocol work over http
what is the application/ipp media type
how is an ipp message encoded
subtitle: How print requests are packed into a binary message and carried over HTTP on port 631.

tldr.problem: The Internet Printing Protocol has an abstract model of printers, jobs and attributes, but clients and printers need an exact byte-level format and a transport to exchange those operations.
tldr.mechanism: Each operation is encoded as a compact binary message with the media type application/ipp, and that message is sent as the body of an HTTP/1.1 POST request, with the reply in the HTTP response.
tldr.outcome: This was an Experimental specification. It was replaced by RFC 2910, which is the version to read for IPP encoding and transport.

today: RFC 2565 is Experimental and has been obsoleted by RFC 2910, so new work should follow that document instead.

sections.title: Two Layers: Operation and Transport
sections.content:
RFC 2565 is one of a set of documents that describe the Internet Printing Protocol (IPP), an application-level protocol for distributed printing. The abstract model (printers, jobs, attributes, operations) lives in RFC 2566, the "IPP model document". This document supplies the encoding.

It describes two layers. The transport layer is an HTTP/1.1 request or response. The operation layer is the message body carried inside it, a single operation request or operation response. The body is given the new media type application/ipp.

The IESG note at the front says this is an Experimental protocol and warns that a later Proposed Standard is expected to differ. In particular it expected stronger authentication and privacy features and an ipp: URL type.
sections.eli5: There is an outer envelope (the web request) and a letter inside (the print message). This document explains how to write both.

sections.title: The Operation Layer Message
sections.content:
Every message starts with a 2-byte version-number (major 1, minor 0 for this protocol, so 0x0100), then a 2-byte operation-id in a request or status-code in a response, then a 4-byte request-id. The request-id lets a client match a response to its request, and a response MUST carry the value from the request. It MUST be greater than zero.

Next come zero or more attribute groups, each introduced by a one-byte delimiter tag and followed by its attributes. A single end-of-attributes-tag is always required, and any document data follows it. All integers are signed, two's-complement and big-endian. They are 1 byte (tags, version), 2 bytes (ids, status codes, lengths) or 4 bytes (values).

The groups are operation, job, printer and unsupported attributes. The operation attributes group MUST come first and appear exactly once. The other groups are optional. A job group can repeat in a Get-Jobs response, one group per job.
sections.eli5: A print message is like a form with fixed boxes at the top (version, what to do, a ticket number), then sections of details, then a stop sign, then the thing to print.

sections.title: Attributes, Tags and Values
sections.content:
Each attribute is a value-tag (1 byte, saying the value's type), a 2-byte name-length, the name, a 2-byte value-length and the value. A multi-valued attribute is written as the first value with its name, followed by additional values whose name-length is 0x0000. The zero-length name is the only mechanism for multi-valued attributes.

The tag decides how to read the bytes. Delimiter tags are 0x01 operation attributes, 0x02 job attributes, 0x03 end of attributes, 0x04 printer attributes and 0x05 unsupported attributes. Value tags include out-of-band values (0x10 unsupported, 0x12 unknown, 0x13 no-value), integers (0x21 integer, 0x22 boolean, 0x23 enum) and character strings such as 0x44 keyword and 0x45 uri.

Integers and enums are always sent in exactly four octets, and a boolean is one byte (0x00 false, 0x01 true). An out-of-band tag MUST have a value-length of 0. Tag 0x7F is reserved for extending types beyond 255 values.
sections.eli5: Each detail has a little label saying what kind of thing it is (a number, a word, a yes or no), then its name, then its value. A second value for the same name just leaves the name blank.

sections.title: Transport over HTTP
sections.content:
HTTP/1.1 is the transport. Each IPP operation MUST use the HTTP POST method, with the target object as the request-URI, and the Content-Type of the body in each request and response MUST be application/ipp. A printer MUST support HTTP on IANA well-known port 631, the IPP default port, and may support others.

Because port 80 remains the default for an HTTP URI, a printer URI using port 631 MUST contain the port explicitly, as in http://forest:631/pinetree.

The target printer or job URI is sent twice: as the HTTP request-URI and as the required printer-uri or job-uri operation attribute. The two need not be identical (one can be relative), but they MUST name the same object, and the one inside the operation MUST be absolute. An IPP server MAY answer early, for example with 100 Continue, so clients must expect that.
sections.eli5: The print message goes to the printer the same way a web form goes to a website, and the printer listens at a special door number, 631.

sections.title: Worked Examples and Media Type Registration
sections.content:
Appendix A walks through byte-by-byte examples: a Print-Job request with the job name foobar, 20 copies and two-sided printing, a successful response, a failure response using status code 0x040B (client-error-attributes-or-values-not-supported), a success response with ignored attributes (status 0x0001), plus Print-URI, Create-Job and Get-Jobs examples.

The last appendix is the registration of the application/ipp media type, which states that messages are self-contained and always contain binary data.
sections.eli5: At the back are sample messages written out piece by piece, so builders can check their own work against them.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The IPP model document defines "privacy" as an implementation of Secure Socket Layer version 3 (SSL3), which this RFC notes is not an IETF standards-track specification. It defines "authentication" as the standard way of carrying IPP in HTTP/1.1, including Digest Access Authentication (RFC 2069). The model document is the primary reference for IPP security.

Section 5.1 describes using a https URI, which connects by default to port 443, and sketches optional connect, disconnect and resume helper functions for SSL sessions. The IESG note also encourages experimentation with TLS as a security layer.
sections.eli5: To keep print jobs private, you wrap the connection in the same lock that secure websites use.

fields.name: version-number
fields.desc: Major and minor version, one byte each; 1.0 here.

fields.name: operation-id / status-code
fields.desc: Operation in a request, status code in a response.

fields.name: request-id
fields.desc: Copied into the response; MUST be greater than zero.

items.label: operation-attributes-tag
items.desc: Operation attributes; MUST come first and appear once.
